blocks.task_summary: Find P(A ∪ B) given P(A) = 0.65, P(B) = 0.75, and P(A ∩ B) = 0.6.
method_path: Apply addition rule: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
Substitute values: 0.65 + 0.75 − 0.6
Compute: 0.8
accepted_alternatives: Venn diagram decomposition: P(A ∪ B) = P(A \ B) + P(A ∩ B) + P(B \ A) = 0.05 + 0.6 + 0.15 = 0.8

blocks.task_summary: Hence, or otherwise, find P(A′ ∩ B′).
method_path: Recognise P(A′ ∩ B′) = P((A ∪ B)′) = 1 − P(A ∪ B)
Substitute: 1 − 0.8
Compute: 0.2
accepted_alternatives: Venn diagram: identify and label the region outside both A and B as 0.2

evidence.basis: recognition that P(A′ ∩ B′) = P((A ∪ B)′) OR = 1 − P(A ∪ B) (region/value may be seen in a correctly shaded/labeled Venn diagram) (M1), = 1 − 0.8 = 0.2 A1

blocks.task_summary: Use S₄ = 40 and S₅ = 65 to find p and q where Sₙ = pn² − qn, by forming two equations from the given sum formula and solving the simultaneous linear system for p and q.
method_path: Substitute n=4, S₄=40 into Sₙ=pn²−qn to obtain 16p−4q=40 → 4p−q=10
Substitute n=5, S₅=65 into Sₙ=pn²−qn to obtain 25p−5q=65 → 5p−q=13
Solve the simultaneous linear equations, e.g., subtract to get p=3, then back-substitute to get q=2
accepted_alternatives: Use arithmetic sequence sum formula Sₙ = n/2(2u₁+(n−1)d) to form equations in u₁ and d, solve to get u₁=1 and d=6, then equate coefficients in Sₙ = 3n²−2n to obtain p=3, q=2.

evidence.basis: METHOD 1: attempt to form at least one equation using S₄ or S₅ (M1); 25p−5q=65 → 5p−q=13 and 40=16p−4q → 10=4p−q (A1); valid attempt to solve simultaneous linear equations in p and q (M1); p=3, q=2 (A1A1). METHOD 2: attempt to form equation using S₄ or S₅ (M1); gives equations in u₁ and d (A1); solve to get u₁=1, d=6 (A1); equate to Sₙ = 3n²−2n giving p=3, q=2 (A1).

blocks.task_summary: Find the fifth term u₅ of the arithmetic sequence using u₅ = S₅ − S₄ = 65 − 40 = 25.
method_path: Compute u₅ = S₅ − S₄
accepted_alternatives: Use u₅ = u₁ + 4d with u₁=1, d=6 giving u₅ = 1 + 4×6 = 25.
Use S₅ = 5(u₁ + u₅)/2 = 65 with u₁=1 to solve for u₅ = 25.

evidence.basis: u₅ = S₅ − S₄ OR substituting u₁ and d into u₅ = u₁ + 4d OR substituting u₁ into S₅ = 5(u₁+u₅)/2 = 65 (M1); u₅ = 65 − 40 = 25 (A1).

blocks.task_summary: Given triangle ABC with AB = 6 cm, AC = 10 cm and cos BÂC = 1/5, find the area of triangle ABC.
method_path: Use sin^2 BÂC = 1 − cos^2 BÂC to express sin BÂC
Compute sin BÂC = sqrt(1 − (1/5)^2) = sqrt(24)/5
Apply area formula A = 1/2 × AB × AC × sin BÂC
Substitute values: A = 1/2 × 10 × 6 × sqrt(24)/5
Simplify to A = 12 cm^2
accepted_alternatives: Method 2: Find perpendicular height of triangle via height = 6 × sin BÂC (using Pythagorean identity) or via Pythagoras' theorem on right triangle with hypotenuse 6 and adjacent 6/5, giving height = 12/5; then Area = 1/2 × base × height = 1/2 × 10 × 12/5 = 12 cm^2.

evidence.basis: METHOD 1: M1 for attempt to use Pythagoras' theorem or Pythagorean identity sin^2α + cos^2α = 1; A1 for sqrt(5^2 − 1^2) = sqrt(24) or sin^2BÂC = 1 − (1/5)^2; A1 for sinBÂC = sqrt(24)/5; M1 for attempt to use Area = 1/2 ab sinC; A1 for 1/2 × 10 × 6 × sqrt(24)/5; A1 for 12 cm^2. [6 marks]

METHOD 2: M1 for attempt to find perpendicular height; M1 for Pythagorean identity or Pythagoras' theorem; A1 for intermediate work; A1 for height = 12/5; M1 for Area = 1/2 × base × height; A1 for 12 cm^2.

blocks.task_summary: The binomial expansion of (1+kx)^n is given as 1+12x+28k^2 x^2+...+k^n x^n with n in positive integers and k real. Find n and k by equating binomial coefficients to the given terms.
method_path: Expand (1+kx)^n via binomial theorem: 1 + nC1 kx + nC2 k^2 x^2 + ...
Equate coefficient of x: nC1 k = 12 gives n k = 12
Equate coefficient of x^2: nC2 = 28 gives n(n-1)/2 = 28
Form quadratic equation: n^2 - n - 56 = 0
Solve: (n-8)(n+7) = 0 gives n = 8
Substitute into n k = 12: k = 12/8 = 3/2
accepted_alternatives: Find n = 8 by identifying the appropriate row in Pascal's triangle rather than solving the quadratic algebraically.

evidence.basis: attempt to apply binomial expansion (M1); n k = 12 (A1); n(n-1)/2 = 28 OR n!/(2!(n-2)!) = 28 (A1)
n^2 - n - 56 = 0 OR n(n-1) = 56; valid attempt to solve (M1); n = 8 A1; k = 3/2 A1

blocks.task_summary: Prove by mathematical induction that 5^(2n) - 2^(3n) is divisible by 17 for all n in Z+.
method_path: Verify base case n=1: 5^2 - 2^3 = 25 - 8 = 17, divisible by 17
Assume true for n=k: 5^(2k) - 2^(3k) = 17s, s integer
Rewrite using inductive hypothesis: 17*5^(2k) + 8(5^(2k) - 2^(3k)) = 17*5^(2k) + 8*17s
Factor 17: 17(5^(2k) + 8s), showing divisibility by 17 for n=k+1
Conclude: true for n=1 and n=k implies n=k+1, therefore true for all n in Z+
accepted_alternatives: Throughout, 5^(2k) and 2^(3k) may be replaced by 25^k and 8^k

evidence.basis: Base case A1, assume true M1, consider n=k+1 M1, expand A1, algebraic manipulation to introduce 17s A1, factor out 17 A1, conclusion R1. Note: Award R1 only if 4 of previous 6 marks earned. Note: 5^(2k) and 2^(3k) may be replaced by 25^k and 8^k throughout.

blocks.task_summary: Given z = 5 + qi satisfies z² + iz = -p + 25i with p, q ∈ ℝ, find the values of p and q.
method_path: Substitute z = 5 + qi into z² + iz = -p + 25i
Expand and collect real and imaginary parts
Equate real parts and imaginary parts to obtain two equations
Solve 10q - 20 = 0 for q
Substitute q = 2 into -q² - p + 25 = 0 to obtain p = -19
accepted_alternatives: Method 2: Use sum and product of roots. Rearrange to z² + iz + p - 25i = 0. Sum of roots = -i, one root is 5 + qi so the other is -5 - qi - i. Equate product (5 + qi)(-5 - qi - i) = -p + 25i and solve real and imaginary parts to get q = 2, p = -19.

evidence.basis: Markscheme shows METHOD 1 with M1 for substituting z, A1 for correct expansion, M1 for equating real/imaginary parts, and A1A1 for q = 2, p = -19. METHOD 2 using sum and product of roots is also accepted with equivalent mark allocation. Total [5 marks].

blocks.task_summary: Find the indefinite integral of x (ln x)^2 dx using integration by parts twice.
method_path: set up integration by parts with u = (ln x)^2, dv = x dx
apply formula integral u dv = uv minus integral v du
simplify to (x^2/2)(ln x)^2 minus integral x ln x dx
apply integration by parts again with u = ln x, dv = x dx
obtain integral x ln x dx = (x^2/2) ln x minus x^2/4
combine: (x^2/2)(ln x)^2 minus (x^2/2) ln x + x^2/4 + c
accepted_alternatives: METHOD 2: integration by parts with u = x ln x, dv = ln x dx, using known result integral ln x dx = x ln x minus x
METHOD 3: integration by parts with u = ln x, dv = x ln x dx, using known result integral x ln x dx = (x^2/2) ln x minus x^2/4

evidence.basis: METHOD 1: attempt to integrate by parts (M1); u = (ln x)^2, dv = x dx (M1); A1 for first application yielding (x^2/2)(ln x)^2 minus integral x ln x dx; attempt to integrate integral x ln x dx by parts with u = ln x (M1); A1 for integral x ln x dx = (x^2/2) ln x minus x^2/4; final A1 for (x^2/2)(ln x)^2 minus (x^2/2) ln x + x^2/4 + c
METHODS 2 and 3 are accepted alternative routes, each marked with the same 6-mark scheme yielding the same final expression

blocks.task_summary: Show that f(x) = sin^2(kx)/x^2 is an even function.
method_path: Evaluate f(-x) = sin^2(k(-x))/(-x)^2
Simplify denominator: (-x)^2 = x^2
Use sin(-kx) = -sin(kx) so sin^2(-kx) = sin^2(kx)
Conclude f(-x) = sin^2(kx)/x^2 = f(x), hence f is even

evidence.basis: M1: f(-x) = sin^2(k(-x))/(-x)^2; A1: = sin^2(-kx)/x^2 = sin^2(kx)/x^2 = f(x), hence f(x) is even AG

blocks.task_summary: Given lim_{x to 0} f(x) = 16, find k by evaluating the limit of sin^2(kx)/x^2 as x approaches 0.
method_path: Recognise limit is indeterminate 0/0
Apply L'Hopital: differentiate numerator sin^2(kx) to k sin(2kx), denominator x^2 to 2x
Simplify to lim k sin(2kx)/(2x), still 0/0
Apply L'Hopital again: numerator to 2k^2 cos(2kx), denominator to 2
Evaluate limit as x to 0: 2k^2/2 = k^2
Set k^2 = 16, solve k = 4 (k > 0)
accepted_alternatives: Maclaurin series: sin(kx) = kx + ..., so sin^2(kx)/x^2 = k^2 + terms in x, limit = k^2 = 16, k = 4
Product of limits: write as (sin(kx)/x)*(sin(kx)/x), each limit = k via L'Hopital or Maclaurin, product = k^2 = 16, k = 4

evidence.basis: METHOD 1: (M1) noting limit is 0/0; M1 attempt differentiate numerator and denominator; A1 lim k sin(2kx)/(2x); M1 attempt differentiate second time; A1 lim 2k^2 cos(2kx)/2 = k^2; A1 k^2=16 so k=4
METHOD 2: M1 attempt Maclaurin series for sin(kx); A1 sin^2(kx) = k^2 x^2 + ...; M1 substitute and take limit; R1 limit = k^2 + terms in x; A1 k^2; A1 k=4
METHOD 3: (M1) split as (sin(kx)/x)*(sin(kx)/x); A1 product of limits; (M1) L'Hopital or Maclaurin for each factor; (A1) each limit = k; A1 product = k^2; A1 k^2=16 so k=4

blocks.task_summary: Show that at the points of intersection of f(x)=ln(2x-9) and g(x)=2ln x-ln d, the x-coordinates satisfy x^2 - 2dx + 9d = 0.

Route via ln(2x-9) = ln(x^2) - ln d giving (2x-9)d = x^2

Note: values for second derivative must be correct to award R marks.

blocks.task_summary: Find the Maclaurin series for cos 2x, then for e^(cos 2x − 1), then for f(x) = e^(cos 2x), each up to and including the term in x⁴.

(ii) substitute series for cos 2x − 1 into series for e^θ and expand: e^(cos2x−1) = 1 − 2x² + (8/3)x⁴ + …
(iii) multiply by e: f(x) = e − 2ex² + (8e/3)x⁴ + …

METHOD 2: (M1) attempt to find Maclaurin series for e^(−2x²) OR e^(2x⁴/3); A1 for correct substitution and product; A1 for final series 1 − 2x² + (8/3)x⁴ + …

simplify to 298e/3000 = 149e/1500

blocks.task_summary: Expand (cosθ + i sinθ)^5 using the binomial theorem and express the result in the form a + bi where a and b are in terms of sinθ and cosθ.
method_path: Apply binomial theorem: (cosθ + i sinθ)^5 = Σ_{r=0}^{5} C(5,r) cos^{5-r}θ (i sinθ)^r
Compute binomial coefficients: 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1

Collect real part a = cos^5θ - 10cos^3θ sin^2θ + 5cosθ sin^4θ
Collect imaginary part b = 5cos^4θ sinθ - 10cos^2θ sin^3θ + sin^5θ

Expansion written with all six terms. A1A1: Award A1 for correct real part and A1 for correct imaginary part. [4 marks]

blocks.task_summary: Using De Moivre's theorem and the result from part (a), show that sin 5θ ≡ 16 sin^5 θ - 20 sin^3 θ + 5 sin θ.
method_path: Apply De Moivre's theorem: (cosθ + i sinθ)^5 = cos5θ + i sin5θ

Obtain sin5θ = 5cos^4θ sinθ - 10cos^2θ sin^3θ + sin^5θ

Note: Some of this working may be seen in part (a). Allow for awarding marks in part (b).

blocks.task_summary: (i) Show that π/5 and 3π/5 are solutions of 16 sin^4 θ - 20 sin^2 θ + 5 = 0. (ii) Hence show that sin(π/5) sin(3π/5) = √5/4.
method_path: (i) Factor sin5θ = sinθ(16sin^4θ - 20sin^2θ + 5) from part (b)
(i) Solve sin5θ = 0 ⇒ 5θ = kπ ⇒ θ = kπ/5, k ∈ Z
(i) Substitute θ = π/5, 3π/5: sin(5·π/5) = sinπ = 0, sin(5·3π/5) = sin3π = 0
(i) Note sin(π/5) ≠ 0, sin(3π/5) ≠ 0, so the quartic factor 16sin^4θ - 20sin^2θ + 5 = 0
(i) Conclude π/5 and 3π/5 are solutions of 16sin^4θ - 20sin^2θ + 5 = 0
(ii) Treat 16sin^4θ - 20sin^2θ + 5 = 0 as quadratic in u = sin^2θ: 16u^2 - 20u + 5 = 0
accepted_alternatives: (c)(ii) Method 2: Use product of four roots of the quartic equation. π/5, 2π/5, 3π/5, 4π/5 are roots; product = 5/16. Recognise sin(π/5)=sin(4π/5) and sin(2π/5)=sin(3π/5), giving sin^2(π/5)sin^2(3π/5)=5/16, so sin(π/5)sin(3π/5)=√5/4.
(c)(ii) Method 3: Treat the quartic as quadratic in sin^2θ with roots sin^2(π/5) and sin^2(3π/5). Product of roots = 5/16, so sin(π/5)sin(3π/5)=√(5/16)=√5/4.

evidence.basis: (c)(i) factorising 16sin^5θ - 20sin^3θ + 5sinθ (M1). sin5θ = sinθ(16sin^4θ - 20sin^2θ + 5). EITHER sin(5·π/5)=0 and sin(5·3π/5)=0 (R1) OR solving sin5θ = 0, 5θ = kπ where k ∈ Z (R1). therefore either sinθ = 0 OR 16sin^4θ - 20sin^2θ + 5 = 0. sin(π/5) ≠ 0 and sin(3π/5) ≠ 0 (R1). therefore π/5, 3π/5 are solutions of 16sin^4θ - 20sin^2θ + 5 = 0 AG. Final R1 dependent on both previous marks.

METHOD 2: Roots of quartic are sin(π/5), sin(2π/5), sin(3π/5), sin(4π/5) (A1). Product of roots = 5/16 (M1)(A1). sin(π/5)=sin(4π/5), sin(2π/5)=sin(3π/5) ⇒ sin^2(π/5)sin^2(3π/5)=5/16 (A1). METHOD 3: Treat as quadratic in sin^2θ (M1). Product of roots sin^2(π/5)·sin^2(3π/5) = 5/16 (M1)(A1)(A1).
